analysis.one_liner: Requires Treasury to break up banks whose collapse would force a taxpayer bailout.
analysis.headline: The bill to break up 'too big to fail' banks was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in April 2013 and never got a hearing or a vote, dying when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Treasury Secretary to publish a list of every commercial bank, investment bank, hedge fund, and insurance company whose collapse would require a taxpayer bailout, then break those firms apart so no single failure could wreck the economy [S2][S3]. It targeted the largest Wall Street institutions, including any U.S. bank holding companies flagged as systemically important by the Financial Stability Board [S3]. The idea behind it: if a company is so big that the government cannot let it fail, ordinary taxpayers end up on the hook for its losses, so it should not be allowed to exist at that size [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and households, who since the 2008 crisis have carried the implicit guarantee that Washington will rescue giant banks with public money. Breaking up the giants would shrink that liability and reduce the concentration of financial power in a handful of firms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers on the hook for bank bailouts

how_it_helps.text: Within 90 days of enactment, Treasury would have to send Congress a 'Too Big to Fail List' naming every commercial bank, investment bank, hedge fund, and insurance company it believes is too big to fail, including U.S. bank holding companies identified as systemically important by the Financial Stability Board [S2][S3].

Beginning one year after enactment, the Treasury Secretary would be required to break up every entity on that list so that its failure would no longer cause a catastrophic effect on the U.S. or global economy without a taxpayer bailout [S2][S3].

The bill's stated purpose is to address 'Too Big to Fail' directly — defining it as any firm so large that its failure would destabilize the financial system or the U.S. economy without substantial government assistance [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest Wall Street banks, investment banks, hedge funds, and insurance companies, which would lose their government backstop and, in many cases, be forced to split into smaller firms. Communities could also face transition costs as giant institutions are reorganized.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the Treasury Secretary sweeping discretion, with no size threshold or criteria specified in the text beyond the 'too big to fail' definition, so which firms get broken up and how would rest almost entirely on one executive branch official's judgment [S3].

Forcing rapid divestiture of the largest banks one year after enactment could disrupt lending, and critics have long argued that large U.S. banks also serve a global role that smaller institutions cannot replace — a cost the bill does not address [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing the implicit taxpayer guarantee behind the largest banks — is real, since the 2008 bailouts shifted private losses onto the public. The main honest objection is design: the bill hands one cabinet secretary broad power to restructure firms without a bright-line size rule, and the one-year deadline could be disruptive. A more careful version of the same idea exists in size-cap proposals the bill did not adopt.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on April 9, 2013, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a Democrat, and never reached the House floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest Wall Street banks and financial conglomerates are better off: because the bill never advanced, none of them face being listed as too big to fail or broken apart by Treasury, and the implicit taxpayer backstop behind them remains intact.

against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with a single Democratic cosponsor and died in committee without a vote, so no roll call exists — but a bill aimed at breaking up the largest banks never advanced in a Republican-controlled House, and its support was entirely from one party.

industries.industry: Megabanks and systemically important bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill would have required Treasury to name them as too big to fail and break them apart, ending the implicit government guarantee that their losses become taxpayer obligations. Their interest in staying at current size runs against the public's interest in not footing bailout bills. [S2][S3]

industries.industry: Large investment banks, hedge funds, and insurance companies
industries.note: The bill covers non-bank financial giants as well, ordering Treasury to break up any firm in these sectors whose failure would require a taxpayer rescue. Its death left their size and government backstop untouched. [S2][S3]
